section.title: You Have Searched Me and Known Me
section.sectionRationale: One of the most intimate psalms in the Psalter, this meditation on God's total knowledge, inescapable presence, and personal forming of every life in the womb stands among the closing Davidic psalms of Book V, its final prayer, search me and know my heart, modeling the self-examination that flows rightly from being fully known and fully loved.
section.thesis: The LORD who knows every thought before it is spoken, who is present in the highest heaven and the darkest depth, who knit the psalmist together in the womb and wrote every day of his life in a book before one of them came to be, is a God whose total knowledge is cause not for dread but for worship, ending in the humble invitation, search me, O God, and lead me in the way everlasting.
section.frameNote: Four stanzas of six verses each mark the psalm's movement: God's total knowledge of me, verses 1-6; God's inescapable presence with me, verses 7-12; God's forming of me in the womb, verses 13-18; and the psalmist's allegiance against evil and invitation to God's searchlight, verses 19-24.

units.label: You have searched me and known me

verses.text: O LORD, You have {{chaqar|searched}} me and known me.
You know when I sit and when I rise; You understand my thoughts from afar.
You search out my path and my lying down; You are aware of all my ways.
Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD.
You hem me in behind and before; You have laid Your hand upon me.
Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, too lofty for me to attain.

units.label: Where can I flee from Your presence

verses.text: Where can I go to escape Your Spirit? Where can I flee from Your presence?
If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there.
If I rise on the wings of the dawn, if I settle by the farthest sea,
even there Your hand will guide me; Your right hand will hold me fast.
If I say, "Surely the darkness will hide me, and the light become night around me,"
even the darkness is not dark to You, but the night shines like the day, for darkness is as light to You.

units.label: You knit me together in my mother's womb

verses.text: For You formed my inmost being; You {{raqam|knit}} me together in my mother's womb.
I praise You, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Marvelous are Your works, and I know this very well.
My frame was not hidden from You when I was made in secret, when I was woven together in the depths of the earth.
Your eyes saw my unformed body; all my days were written in Your book and ordained for me before one of them came to be.
How precious to me are Your thoughts, O God, how vast is their sum!
If I were to count them, they would outnumber the grains of sand; and when I awake, I am still with You.

units.label: Search me, O God, and know my heart
units.note: allegiance against evil, and God's searchlight invited

verses.text: O God, that You would slay the wicked, away from me, you bloodthirsty men,
who speak of You deceitfully; Your enemies take Your name in vain.
Do I not hate those who hate You, O LORD, and detest those who rise against You?
I hate them with perfect hatred; I count them as my enemies.
Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and know my concerns.
See if there is any offensive way in me; lead me in the {{olam|way everlasting}}.

chaqar.gloss: To search out, to probe thoroughly, used of mining into rock. God's searching is not a suspicious investigation but a thorough, intimate knowledge of every corner of a life, which David finds too wonderful to fully grasp, verse 6.

raqam.gloss: To weave or embroider, used here of God knitting the psalmist together in the womb. The image is of careful, skilled handiwork, God as artisan forming every unborn child with the same personal attention He gives every other part of creation.

olam.gloss: Everlasting, ancient, without end. The way everlasting is both the enduring path of righteousness and, ultimately, the path that leads into eternal life with God, the goal of David's closing prayer to be searched, tested, and led.

basic.context: David marvels that the LORD already knows every thought, word, and movement of his life before it happens, is present in the highest heaven and the deepest darkness alike, and personally formed him in the womb, writing every day of his life in a book before any of them began.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm is a meditation, not a philosophical treatise; David describes what it feels like to be fully known by an all-knowing, ever-present, personally involved Creator, and moves from that description to a prescriptive response: hatred of evil aligned with God's own heart, and humble invitation for God to search and lead him.
basic.originalLanguages: God has chaqar, searched, David thoroughly, the same word used for mining deep into rock, yet this searching feels too wonderful, too lofty to attain, verse 6. In the womb God raqam, knit, wove David together with the care of a skilled artisan. The psalm closes asking to be led in the way olam, everlasting, both a lifelong path of righteousness and the path into eternal life.
basic.typology: David's confession that God's eyes saw his unformed body and ordained every day before one of them came to be, verses 15-16, anticipates the New Testament's teaching that believers were chosen and known by God before the foundation of the world, Ephesians 1:4, and that Christ Himself was known before He was formed in Mary's womb, Luke 1:31-35.
basic.christ: The searching, ever-present God of this psalm is revealed in Christ, who knew what was in man without needing to be told, John 2:24-25, and who invites the same searching self-examination David seeks, testing hearts even now, Revelation 2:23, while offering grace to those He finds and forgives.
basic.god: God is shown as fully omniscient, knowing every thought before it forms, fully present everywhere, from the heights of heaven to the depths of Sheol, and fully involved as Creator, personally forming every human life in the womb and writing its days before they begin.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 1:5 echoes God's knowledge of a person before formation in the womb. Hebrews 4:13 restates that nothing in creation is hidden from God's sight. Ephesians 2:10 grounds human dignity and purpose in being God's handiwork. Revelation 2:23 shows Christ Himself searching hearts and minds.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's vision of a God who knows every thought, is present everywhere, and personally forms every life in the womb runs through the whole Bible's insistence on human dignity from conception onward, and finds its fulfillment in Christ, who both searches hearts perfectly and, having been formed in a womb Himself, leads all who invite His searchlight into the way everlasting.

context.literary:
Psalm 139 is one of the most carefully shaped poems in the Psalter, and its structure is the key to its meaning. It falls into four stanzas of six verses each: verses 1 to 6 on God's knowing, verses 7 to 12 on God's presence, verses 13 to 18 on God's making, and verses 19 to 24 on the poet's response to evil and his prayer. The psalm moves from 'You know' to 'You are there' to 'You formed' and then to a plea in the imperative, 'Search me.' Knowledge, presence and creation are not three separate topics but three ways in which one God holds one life.

An inclusio holds the whole thing together. The first verse says, 'O LORD, You have searched me and known me.' The last stanza ends, 'Search me, O God, and know my heart.' The same two verbs, search and know, open and close the psalm. What begins as a statement of fact ends as an invitation. The man who was disturbed by being known has learned to ask for it.

The poem addresses God directly throughout, in the second person, so that 'You' occurs again and again. It is a prayer, not a lecture about God, even in its most theological lines. A second pattern is the play with 'if.' In verses 8 to 12 the poet imagines five escapes, ascending to heaven, making a bed in Sheol, taking the wings of dawn, settling by the farthest sea, and hoping that darkness will cover him, and each is answered with 'even there.' The movement runs high, low, east, west and finally into the dark, a merism covering all space and light.

The shift in verses 19 to 22 is abrupt. After the gentle wonder of verses 13 to 18, the psalm bursts into a violent prayer against the wicked. Readers often treat it as a clumsy insertion, but the literary logic is that a person who has just been overwhelmed by God's holiness cannot sit comfortably beside those who despise it. The last two verses then turn the same searching light inward: the poet first condemns evil outside himself and then asks God to look at himself, which is the proper order of a prayer that does not excuse its writer.
context.historical:
The title reads 'For the choirmaster. Of David. A psalm,' and Israel's tradition has attributed it to David. The Hebrew of the psalm contains a number of forms that scholars have noticed as unusual and as close to Aramaic, which has fed a long argument about whether it was composed late or reflects a stage of the language that David's time already knew. That argument cannot be settled here. What can be said is that the psalm was received as part of the Davidic collection, and that its themes, a king who knows what it is to be hunted and watched, fit the reign of a man who was forced to flee from Saul and whose enemies were many.

The first hearers lived in a world in which gods were thought to be local. A deity belonged to a hill, a river, a city or a people, and to leave the land was to leave the god. The psalm is bold in saying that the LORD cannot be escaped by distance. Jonah's flight from 'the presence of the LORD,' Jonah 1:3, was a failed attempt to do what the poet says cannot be done. Amos made the same point in a prophecy of judgment, that those who dig down to Sheol or climb to heaven will be found, Amos 9:2-3. For a people who had been taken into exile, as the psalm's later readers were, it was good news as well as sobering news: God had not stayed in Jerusalem when they left it.

The imagery of 'woven together in the depths of the earth,' verse 15, reflects the common idea that the womb is a hidden place akin to the earth itself, from which humanity came. Genesis 2:7 had the man formed from the dust and Job 1:21 speaks of returning 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return,' using the earth and the womb in a single picture. The weaving language, from the craft of the embroiderer, was also at home in a culture where the tabernacle's curtains were embroidered work.

Sheol, the place of the dead, was understood as the lowest point, far from the temple and from the praise of God. That God is present even there, verse 8, was an astonishing claim that Proverbs 15:11 echoes when it says Sheol and Abaddon are open before the LORD.
context.canonical:
Psalm 139 stands in the last Davidic collection and is read alongside Psalm 138's thanks and Psalm 140's prayer for rescue. It gathers several strands of Old Testament teaching about God's nature. The omniscience of the LORD appears in Proverbs 15:11, in Jeremiah 23:23-24, where the LORD asks whether a man can hide in secret places, and in 1 Kings 8:39, where Solomon asks God to act on His knowledge of every heart. Job 14:5 speaks of days determined and months numbered, which is the thought of verse 16.

The creation language is shared with Job. Job 10:8-12 uses much the same language as verses 13 to 15, including shaping, forming and knitting with bones and sinews, but Job uses it as a charge that God made him only to destroy him, while David uses it as praise. The two texts are a pair: the same truth can be a ground of complaint in suffering or of worship in peace, and the whole canon keeps both voices. Jeremiah 1:5 and Isaiah 49:1 speak of being known and named from the womb, and Paul takes up the same note about his calling in Galatians 1:15.

The New Testament does not quote Psalm 139 directly, but its themes pervade it. Hebrews 4:13 says nothing in all creation is hidden from God's sight. Paul in Athens says God is 'not far from each one of us,' Acts 17:27. Romans 8:27 says God searches hearts and knows the mind of the Spirit. First Corinthians 13:12 gives the believer's hope of knowing 'fully, even as I am fully known.' Jesus' teaching that the very hairs of the head are numbered, Luke 12:7, belongs to the same picture. The prayer for the wicked to be removed meets Jesus' command to love enemies, and the psalm's last prayer, 'lead me in the way everlasting,' is answered in the One who calls Himself 'the way,' John 14:6.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet intends to take a doctrine that is easy to state and make it personal. Every Israelite knew that God sees everything. David wants them to feel what that means when it is addressed to oneself: every sitting and rising, every thought before it forms, every word before it is spoken, is already known. The first response is awe, 'too wonderful for me,' verse 6, and the first temptation is escape, verse 7. The psalm leads the reader through that temptation to a better place.

He wants his hearers to see that being known is not a threat for a person who belongs to God. The same hand that hems him in, verse 5, also guides and holds him, verse 10. The God who sees the dark is the God who made the body and wrote its days, and a creature has nothing to fear from a Maker who has loved him since before he was born.

He also intends to draw a moral line. A person who is gripped by God's presence cannot treat God's enemies lightly. Verses 19 to 22 are not private spite. They are the loyalty of someone who has just been overwhelmed by God's holiness and finds it intolerable that His name should be abused. The final prayer shows what the poet really fears: not his foes but himself. He asks God to test him, so that the first thing he is willing to hand over to be searched is his own heart.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what a believer says about God and about himself in a moment of reflection. The statements about God, His knowledge, presence and creative care, are meant to be believed by every reader. The prayer of verses 23 and 24 is a pattern that can be prayed by anyone. The poet's reaction of wonder and his plea for guidance are an example to be followed.

The description of the poet's own hatred is a different matter. Verses 21 and 22 describe how David felt, and the Bible does not simply command every reader to repeat them. The New Testament asks believers to love their enemies and pray for those who mistreat them, Luke 6:27-28, and Paul tells them not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, Romans 12:19. What does carry forward is the part of the psalm that shares God's own concern for His name and His justice, hating evil in the sense Paul commands in Romans 12:9, 'Detest what is evil.' The person who prays the psalm today must separate the zeal for God from any desire for personal revenge.

The language of verses 13 to 16 about the womb should be read as praise, not as a legal text. It affirms that God is involved in the making of each person, and it has therefore been used in discussion of the value of life before birth. That application seems fair, since the psalm treats the unborn child as already the object of God's seeing and planning, but the psalm itself does not set out a policy, and readers should be careful to argue from its principle, not to claim that it says more than it says.

debates.question: How should Christians read the hatred of verses 19 to 22?

views.label: A fitting zeal for God that Christians can pray in a redirected form
views.case: The poet is not speaking of private vengeance. He lays the matter before God and asks God to act, which is how Romans 12:19 says believers should treat injustice. Hating those who hate God is a way of siding with God, and the church can pray for God to end violence and defeat evil, as it does in Revelation 6:10.

views.label: A sub-Christian outlook that the New Testament corrects
views.case: Jesus commanded love for enemies, Matthew 5:44, and rebuked James and John when they wished to call fire on a village, Luke 9:54-55. On this reading the psalm is honest but belongs to an earlier and incomplete stage of revelation, and Christians should not repeat it as it stands.

views.label: Hatred of evil rather than of persons
views.case: The 'perfect hatred' of verse 22 is a complete rejection of what God opposes. The word names a settled moral loyalty, and the enemies are identified by what they do, speaking deceitfully and rising against God. The psalm then turns the lens on itself in verse 24, 'See if there is any offensive way in me,' and so does not exempt the poet from the same judgment.

debates.bearing: All three readers treat the passage as honest prayer given to God, not an instruction to harm anyone. The safest reading holds that hatred of evil belongs with trust in God's justice, and that Christ's command to love enemies governs how the church acts.

debates.question: What does it mean that all my days were 'written in Your book' and 'ordained' in verse 16?

views.label: God fixes the length and content of each life
views.case: Job 14:5 speaks of days determined and the number of months set with God. On this reading verse 16 says every day of a person's life was recorded before any of them began, and the verse is a source of comfort that no life is outside His plan.

views.label: God had a plan for the formation of the body
views.case: The context of verses 13 to 16 is about being made in the womb, and the verse begins with the 'unformed body.' Some take the 'book' as the plan in which the parts and days of formation were set down, so that the line is about God's care in making and not a doctrine of the whole of life.

views.label: God's foreknowledge without cancelling human choice
views.case: Scripture holds God's sovereignty and human responsibility together, as Acts 17:26-28 does when it speaks of appointed times and a God who is near. The psalm affirms that God sees everything in advance, and it still prays in verse 24 for guidance, which presupposes real choosing.

debates.bearing: Each view accepts that God knew and cared for the person before birth. The verse is meant to comfort, not to answer the philosophical question of freedom, and readers should hold it as a promise of care rather than as a formula for fate.

debates.question: Is 'Your Spirit' in verse 7 the Holy Spirit?

views.label: God's own presence and life
views.case: The parallel line, 'Your presence,' shows the two phrases mean the same thing: God Himself in His nearness. The psalm does not develop the Spirit as a distinct person and the line would be no more than a poetic way of speaking of God.

views.label: The Holy Spirit as a person
views.case: Christian readers have long heard in the line the same Spirit who searches the deep things of God, 1 Corinthians 2:10-11, and who is given to believers. Psalm 51:11 and Psalm 143:10 also speak of God's Spirit within a prayer for guidance.

debates.bearing: The psalm's own parallel favours the first reading in its setting, while the doctrine of the Trinity gives the second reading a firm place in Christian reflection. The point for both is that God's own presence cannot be escaped.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb 'search' in verses 1 and 23 is chaqar, which means to dig down, probe and examine thoroughly. It is used of mining for ore in Job 28:3 and of searching out the matter with care in Proverbs 25:2. The psalm uses it for the way God investigates a person, and it forms the inclusio of the poem. Paired with it is yada, 'know,' which in Hebrew means more than information. To 'know' is to be personally acquainted, and the verb recurs in verses 1, 2, 4, 14 and 23. In verse 14 the poet says 'I know this very well,' as if to say that what God has known of him he has now begun to know of God.

The picture in verse 5, 'You hem me in,' uses a verb that elsewhere means to besiege a city. The same verb appears for a city under siege in 2 Kings 17:5. Here the siege is not hostile but protective, with God behind and before and His hand laid upon the poet. The same verse can be heard as threat or comfort, and verses 7 to 12 show that David first hears threat and then comfort.

Verse 13 says God formed 'my inmost being,' and the BSB footnote reads 'Hebrew my kidneys.' In the Old Testament the kidneys were the seat of the deepest feelings and conscience, as in Psalm 26:2 and Jeremiah 17:10, where the BSB's 'mind' renders the same word and God tests heart and kidneys. The psalm means that God made the very centre of the self. The verb 'knit' is a form of the verb for covering or screening, and some take it as 'covered me,' which would give the womb as a protective cover. In either reading the line speaks of intimate and careful making. In verse 15 the verb 'woven' is the word for embroidery, the work of a skilled craftsman in coloured thread, which is the kind of work used for the tabernacle curtains in Exodus 26:36. The womb is called 'the depths of the earth,' which recalls the formation of Adam from the soil in Genesis 2:7.

Verse 14 says 'fearfully and wonderfully made.' The word for 'wonderfully' is a form of the root pala, to be extraordinary, which is used of God's wonders in the exodus in Exodus 3:20. The word translated 'fearfully' is the plural of the root meaning to fear or revere, and the sense is that the maker's work provokes awe. The psalm uses the same root for the 'too wonderful' knowledge of verse 6, so that God's knowing and God's making are called by the same word.

In verse 16 the word for 'unformed body,' golmi, is found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. It points to something rolled up, a form not yet shaped, so that the poet speaks of what God saw before there was anything to see. Verse 22's 'perfect hatred' uses a word for completeness or full measure, taklit, which suggests total commitment, not extreme heat. Finally 'offensive way' in verse 24 is literally a way of pain or grief, which is how the poet describes the harm of sin.

typology.type: The poet searched and known by God, verses 1 and 23
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament pictured God searching hearts, Jeremiah 17:10, and the New Testament says Christ holds that role: 'I am the One who searches minds and hearts,' Revelation 2:23. Jesus knew what was in man without needing anyone to tell Him, John 2:24-25, and Hebrews 4:12-13 says the word of God judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart. The escalation is that the Searcher took on flesh and bore what He found. The type falls short in that the poet could only ask to be examined, whereas Christ both examines and bears the guilt the search discovers.

typology.type: No escape from God's presence, verses 7 to 10
typology.fulfillment: The psalm's picture of God in heaven and in Sheol is fulfilled in the Son's descent and ascent. Paul writes of the One who 'descended to the lower parts of the earth' and 'ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things,' Ephesians 4:9-10. Christ went to the depths and to the highest place, so that nowhere lies outside His reach. The correspondence is with the movement of the incarnate Christ, not a claim that the psalm is about Him. The pattern also falls short, since the psalm describes where God already is, whereas the gospel describes God coming to us.

typology.type: The womb as 'the depths of the earth,' verse 15
typology.fulfillment: The poet draws on the language of the earth as the place of hiddenness and origin. In the New Testament Jesus is formed in the womb of Mary by the Spirit, Luke 1:35, and later laid in the earth in a tomb and raised, as Jonah was in the belly of the fish, Matthew 12:40. The first man was made from earth, and the last Adam gave Himself to the earth, 1 Corinthians 15:45-47. The correspondence is loose and works by theme. It falls short as a type since the psalm is about every person made by God, and the link with Christ is by extension.

typology.type: The prayer 'lead me in the way everlasting,' verse 24
typology.fulfillment: The 'way' of Israel's wisdom, Psalm 1:6, becomes in the New Testament a Person. Jesus says, 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6, and early believers were called people of 'the Way,' Acts 9:2. The poet asks God to lead; the gospel answers that He has come to lead in His own Person and has gone ahead through death to the Father. The type falls short because the psalm asks for guidance on a path not yet opened, while Christ's followers walk a path He has already completed.

study.christ:
Psalm 139 is not quoted of Jesus in the New Testament, and a careful reader will not claim more. But the psalm leads to Him by theme, by contrast, and by the fulfilment of its hopes.

The first link is the searching of the heart. The psalm trembles before a God who knows its thoughts before they are spoken, and the Gospels show Jesus doing precisely that. He knew what was in man, John 2:24-25. He read the reasoning of the scribes in their hearts, Mark 2:8, and told Nathanael what he had done under the fig tree, John 1:48. In Revelation He says, 'I am the One who searches minds and hearts,' Revelation 2:23, using the same language as Jeremiah 17:10 where it belongs to the LORD. The psalm's God and Jesus are the same searching Lord.

The second link is the question of presence. David asks, 'Where can I flee from Your presence?' and the Old Testament answer is that nowhere is outside God's reach. The New Testament says that this presence came near. 'The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. Jesus, just before ascending, promised, 'surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age,' Matthew 28:20. The God who is in heaven and in Sheol came into both, and Paul says the One who 'descended to the lower parts of the earth' is the very One who 'ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things,' Ephesians 4:9-10.

Third is the matter of fear. The poet begins with unease at being seen and ends by asking to be seen. What makes that move possible, from hiding to openness, is the gospel. Adam hid among the trees, Genesis 3:8, and the sinner who is uncovered before a holy God has reason to flee. In Christ, there is 'no condemnation,' Romans 8:1, and believers can come to the throne of grace with confidence, Hebrews 4:16. Hebrews 4:13 says everything is uncovered and exposed before God, and the next verse offers the High Priest who sympathises with weakness. The comfort of being fully known is that the one who knows is the one who has taken the penalty.

Finally, the poem ends with 'the way everlasting,' and Jesus names Himself as the way. David's last prayer is answered in the Person who leads His people through death into the Father's presence, so that 'when I awake, I am still with You,' verse 18, is something Paul can describe with a Christian hope, 1 Thessalonians 4:17.

A caution is needed about verse 15 and 16. The psalm is about every human being, and it should not be pressed into a prediction of the incarnation. The links to Christ rest on what the New Testament says about Him, not on hidden allegories in the womb language.
study.god:
Few chapters of the Bible teach the doctrine of God's knowledge and nearness as personally as this one. It also shows what kind of God He is by what He does with His knowledge.

He knows completely. The psalm moves through the whole of a day: sitting and rising, the path and the lying down, thoughts 'from afar' and words before they are spoken, verses 2 to 4. Nothing about the person is outside the knowing, the outward and the inward, the public and the hidden. That knowledge is not general. It is addressed to one man by name: 'You have searched me.' Theology calls this omniscience, but the psalm never uses the abstract word; it speaks of being known.

He is present everywhere, though not in the way a spread-out thing is present. The psalm names the heavens, Sheol, the dawn, the sea, and the darkness, and says God is in each. This is not a statement that God is everything, but that nothing is outside His reach, as Jeremiah 23:24 says when God asks, 'Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?' Solomon had said that the highest heavens cannot contain Him, 1 Kings 8:27. The psalm adds that His presence is not only vast but personal: His hand guides and holds.

He is the Creator in detail. The same God who spread the heavens knitted a child in the womb, verses 13 to 15. The psalm links greatness and intimacy. Because He made me, He knows me, and because He knows me, He cannot be fooled. Creation grounds knowledge.

He is light. 'Even the darkness is not dark to You,' verse 12, and John says 'God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all,' 1 John 1:5. This is a moral as well as a physical claim, which is why the psalm turns in verse 19 to those who speak against Him.

He is holy, which is why the poet's attitude to evil is so sharp, and He is just, for the psalm asks Him to deal with the wicked. But He is also the God to whom a person can say, 'Search me.' He is not hostile to being examined, because His aim is to lead 'in the way everlasting.'

Worship in response is a mixture of wonder, trust and honesty. The psalm models wonder, 'Marvelous are Your works,' verse 14. It models trust, resting in a hand that holds. And it models honesty, inviting the Searcher to find what the poet cannot see. A person who sings this psalm declines to hide, declines to boast, and agrees to be led.

crossReferences.note: God asks whether a man can hide in secret places where He cannot see him, and whether He does not fill the heavens and the earth. It sets out in the prophet's voice the claim Psalm 139:7-12 makes in the poet's. Both deny any hiding place from God.

Jonah got up to flee 'away from the presence of the LORD.' His escape attempt is the story that Psalm 139:7 answers in advance. The sea he fled across was itself under God's hand, and the narrative shows that distance does not change God's reach.

Though they dig down to Sheol or climb to heaven, or hide on Carmel or at the sea's floor, God will find them. This is the same sweep of places as Psalm 139:8-10 but turned into a warning to the rebellious, where the psalmist receives it as comfort.

Job also speaks of being shaped, molded and knit together with bones and sinews, but he asks whether his maker will now destroy him. Psalm 139:13-16 uses similar language as praise. The two texts show that the same truth about God's making can be spoken in lament or in worship.

Before God formed Jeremiah in the womb He knew him and set him apart. This gives to one prophet what Psalm 139:13-16 says of every person, that God's knowledge reaches back before birth. It lets readers see the psalm as an ordinary truth and Jeremiah as a particular call.

Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD, how much more the hearts of men. It is a compact version of Psalm 139's argument: if God sees the deepest place of the dead, He certainly sees the hearts of the living.

The word of God judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart, and nothing in creation is hidden from God's sight. It applies the teaching of Psalm 139:1-4 to the church, adding that those who are exposed also have a High Priest to approach.

Paul tells the Athenians that God determined appointed times and boundaries, and that He is not far from each one, since in Him we live and move. This echoes Psalm 139's sense that God's presence and planning are close to every person.

Believers are not to avenge themselves, but to leave room for God's wrath, and to overcome evil with good. It governs how Psalm 139:19-22 is prayed in the church: the wish for God to deal with evil is handed over to Him and joined with love for enemies.

Now I know in part, then I shall know fully, even as I am fully known. It treats being known by God as the standard of the believer's final knowledge, which fits the psalm's amazement at the Lord's knowing and its hope to be with Him when it awakes.

David asks the LORD to test him, try him and examine his heart and mind. It is the same request as Psalm 139:23-24, asked on the ground of his integrity. Taken together the two prayers show that David prayed openly for God's scrutiny on more than one occasion.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question that begins in Genesis 3. When the man and woman ate the fruit they heard the LORD walking in the garden and hid, Genesis 3:8, and the Lord's first question to them was, 'Where are you?' Since then humanity has tried to leave God's gaze. Psalm 139 is the confession of a person who has learnt that hiding is impossible and has begun to stop. It is the answer of the redeemed to the question the first couple evaded.

It also continues the story of God's creative care. The poet's sense of being made in secret, formed from the earth, takes the reader back to Genesis 1 and 2, where God makes humanity in His image and breathes into the dust. The psalm holds each person as an individual instance of that making. Genesis 1:27 does not stop at the first man and woman; it continues in every womb.

Forward from the psalm the story gives the poet's hopes new weight. The prophets look for the day when 'they will all know Me,' Jeremiah 31:34, because God will write His law on hearts. The poet's request, 'Search me,' becomes the heartbeat of the new covenant. In Christ, God's searching light is paired with forgiveness, and in the Spirit it becomes a presence within, Romans 8:9.

At the end of the story the picture of verses 18 and 24 comes true. The poet's cry, 'When I awake, I am still with You,' is realised in resurrection, and the 'way everlasting' ends in a city where there is no night, Revelation 21:25, and where God's servants will see His face, Revelation 22:4. In that city nothing needs to be hidden, since nothing unclean enters, and nothing is lost to the God who numbered every day. What the psalm shows in doubt and wonder, the new creation shows without a veil: to be fully known and fully loved by the One who made us is the end of the story, not its terror, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

sermon.title: Doing the Right Thing Never Ruins Your Life: A Belief That Prevents Abortion
sermon.why: Piper works directly from Psalm 139:13-16 to show that God's forming and knowing of a person in the womb grounds the sanctity of unborn life, applying the psalm's central confession pastorally and practically, exactly the value of human life this psalm is meant to teach.

quiz.q: What does David marvel at in verses 1-6?

options.text: That the LORD already knows his every thought, word, and movement before they happen, knowledge too wonderful for him to attain.
options.note: Verses 1-6 describe total, intimate divine knowledge that leaves David in awe rather than dread.

options.text: That God cannot know his private thoughts.
options.note: The passage says the opposite, that God knows a word before it is even on David's tongue, verse 4.

options.text: That other people know him better than God does.
options.note: The entire stanza contrasts God's superior, total knowledge with any human knowledge of David.

options.text: That God's knowledge of him will end when he dies.
options.note: The psalm assumes ongoing knowledge and presence, extending even into Sheol, verse 8, not a limit at death.

quiz.q: According to verses 7-12, where can a person go to escape God's presence?

options.text: Nowhere, God is present in the highest heavens, the depths of Sheol, the farthest sea, and even in darkness.
options.note: The stanza systematically lists every extreme, height, depth, distance, darkness, to show God's presence is inescapable.

options.text: In the darkness, since darkness hides a person from God.
options.note: Verse 12 explicitly says darkness is not dark to God, but shines like the day to Him.

options.text: Only in foreign lands outside Israel's borders.
options.note: The imagery is cosmic, heaven, Sheol, sea, not limited to national borders.

options.text: In the depths of the sea alone, but nowhere else.
options.note: The sea is only one of several places named; God's presence extends everywhere the psalm mentions.

quiz.q: What does David confess about his forming in the womb, verses 13-16?

options.text: That God personally knit him together, saw his unformed body, and wrote all his days in His book before any of them began.
options.note: Verses 13-16 describe God's intimate, purposeful involvement in forming David before birth.

options.text: That his formation in the womb was purely a random biological accident with no divine involvement.
options.note: The passage explicitly credits God with forming, knitting, and ordaining David's days from before birth.

options.text: That God only became interested in him after he was born.
options.note: The text says God's eyes saw him while still unformed, before birth, not only afterward.

options.text: That his days were left undetermined until he chose them himself.
options.note: Verse 16 says his days were written and ordained before one of them came to be, not left to be self-determined.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's closing request in verses 23-24?

options.text: Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me and see if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.
options.note: This closing prayer is the natural response of someone already fully known, inviting further examination and guidance.

options.text: A request that God stop searching him and leave him alone.
options.note: The prayer is the opposite, an invitation for God to search and examine even more closely.

options.text: A demand that God punish David's enemies immediately.
options.note: That request appears earlier, verses 19-22; the closing prayer turns inward toward self-examination and guidance.

options.text: A request for wealth and long life above all else.
options.note: The closing request is for moral examination and guidance in righteousness, not material blessing.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's teaching on being formed in the womb connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates believers being chosen and known by God before the foundation of the world, and Christ Himself being formed and known in Mary's womb.
options.note: Ephesians 1:4 and Luke 1:31-35 both extend this psalm's confession of God's purposeful forming of life before birth.

options.text: It has no connection to any New Testament teaching.
options.note: Passages like Ephesians 1:4 and Jeremiah 1:5 directly echo this psalm's theology of being known before formation.

options.text: It only applies to David personally and to no one else.
options.note: Scripture applies this same truth broadly, to Jeremiah, to believers generally, and to Christ Himself.

options.text: It contradicts Jeremiah's account of being known before birth.
options.note: Jeremiah 1:5 closely parallels rather than contradicts this psalm's claim of being known before formation.

questions: David finds it comforting, not threatening, that God knows every thought before it forms. Does God's total knowledge of you feel like comfort or dread right now, and why?
There is nowhere David can go, height, depth, or darkness, to escape God's presence. Where do you find yourself trying to hide from God, and what would it mean to trust His presence there instead?
David praises God for personally forming him in the womb, before birth. How does this shape the way you think about the value of every unborn life, including your own?
David's zeal against evil in verses 19-22 flows from love for God's honor, not personal grudge. Where might your own anger need to be examined to see whether it serves God's glory or your own pride?
The psalm ends with an invitation, search me, O God, and lead me in the way everlasting. What would it look like this week to actually invite God's searchlight into a specific area of your life?

translationNotes.note: Inmost being renders a Hebrew word literally meaning kidneys, an idiom for the seat of one's deepest inner self, similar to how English uses heart.
How precious to me are Your thoughts carries a footnote possibility, how amazing are Your thoughts concerning me, both readings expressing wonder at the vastness and personal focus of God's thoughts.

Your enemies take Your name in vain is textually difficult; a footnote notes the Hebrew could also be read as Your enemies take Your cities in vain, though the sense of irreverent misuse of God's name fits the surrounding verses best.
